description_full: Power Solutions International, Inc. designs, engineers, manufactures, markets, and sells engines and power systems in the United States, the rest of North America, the Pacific Rim, Europe, and internationally. The company offers basic engine blocks integrated with fuel system parts, as well as completely packaged power systems, that include combinations of front accessory drives, cooling systems, electronic systems, air intake systems, fuel systems, housings, power takeoff systems, exhaust systems, hydraulic systems, enclosures, brackets, hoses, tubes, packaging, telematics, and other assembled componentry. It also designs and manufactures large, custom-engineered integrated electrical power generation systems for standby and prime power applications; sells emission-certified compression ignition and spark-ignition internal combustion engines; designs and fabricates power system enclosures; and sources electrification components. In addition, the company provides mobile and stationary gensets for emergency standby, rental, prime power, demand response, microgrid, oil and gas, data center, renewable energy resiliency, and combined heat and power; forklifts, wood chippers, stump grinders, sweepers/industrial scrubbers, aerial lift platforms/scissor lifts, irrigation pumps, oil and gas compression, oil lifts, off road utility vehicles, ground support equipment, ice resurfacing equipment, pump jacks, and battery packs; vocational trucks and vans, school buses, transit buses, and terminal and utility tractors; and internal aftermarket and OEM-developed service parts programs. It serves original equipment manufacturers and end-user customers across the power systems, industrial, and transportation end-markets; and large and multinational organizations. The company was founded in 1985 and is headquartered in Wood Dale, Illinois.

financial_summary: Power Solutions International,  is a small-cap industrials business with a $897M market cap on $722M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +14% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 31% against a 10% cost of capital — a 21-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 18% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $14M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.21×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
Accruals are elevated at +21.2% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 16× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 63% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.
